As I reached through the valve with a cup of water for the old cat, my shirtsleeves caught in the loop supporting the basket. In an instant I had pulled it loose from the bottom. It vanished so suddenly that it might as well have dissolved into thin air. I am certain that less than a tenth of a second passed between the basket coming free and its complete disappearance, together with everything inside it. I sent my good wishes after it towards the earth, but of course I had no hope that the cat or her kittens could survive to tell the story of their bad luck.

“At six o’clock I noticed that a large part of the earth visible to the east lay in deep shadow. The darkness spread quickly, and by five minutes to seven it covered the entire surface I could see. Yet the setting sun continued to shine on the balloon for a long time afterwards. Though I had fully expected this, it gave me enormous pleasure. Clearly, in the morning I would see the sun rise at least several hours before the people of Rotterdam, despite their being much farther east. Day after day, as I climbed higher, I would enjoy longer and longer stretches of sunlight. I decided to begin a journal of the journey, counting each day continuously from one hour to twenty-four, without allowing the periods of darkness to affect the count.

“At ten o’clock I felt sleepy and decided to lie down for the rest of the night. Only then did a problem occur to me which, obvious as it may seem, I had completely overlooked until that very moment. If I went to sleep, how would the air inside the chamber be renewed while I slept? I could not possibly keep breathing it for longer than an hour at most. Even if I could stretch that time to an hour and a quarter, the consequences might be disastrous. This problem troubled me greatly. It may be hard to believe that, after all the dangers I had already survived, I took this difficulty so seriously that I abandoned hope of reaching my final goal and decided I would have to descend. But my uncertainty lasted only a moment.

The Attorney General informed the jury that the prisoner before them, though young in age, had long experience in the acts of treason for which his life was now forfeit. His communications with the nation’s enemy had not begun today, yesterday, last year, or even the year before. It was certain that, for longer than that, he had regularly travelled between France and England on secret business for which he could offer no honest explanation. If treachery were capable of prospering—which, fortunately, it never was—the true wickedness and criminal nature of this business might have escaped discovery. Providence, however, had inspired a fearless person of irreproachable character to investigate the prisoner’s plans and, horrified by what he found, report them to His Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and most honourable Privy Council. This patriot would appear before the jury. His conduct and position were, taken as a whole, sublime. He had once been the prisoner’s friend, but in an hour at once fortunate and terrible he had discovered his disgraceful activities. He had then resolved to sacrifice, upon his country’s sacred altar, the traitor he could no longer hold dear. If Britain, like ancient Greece and Rome, officially awarded statues to public benefactors, this outstanding citizen would surely have received one. Since Britain did not, he probably would not. Virtue, as the poets had observed in many passages the Attorney General knew the jury could recite word for word—here the jurors’ faces betrayed their guilty awareness that they knew no such passages—was in some sense infectious. This applied particularly to the radiant virtue called patriotism, or love of one’s country. The noble example of this spotless, unquestionable witness for the Crown, whom it was an honour even to mention inadequately, had inspired the prisoner’s servant. It had awakened in him a sacred resolve to search his master’s desk drawers and pockets and secretly take his papers. The Attorney General expected some attempt to discredit this admirable servant. In general, however, he preferred the man to his own brothers and sisters and respected him more than his own father and mother. He confidently invited the jury to feel the same. The testimony of these two witnesses, together with the documents they had uncovered and which would be presented in court, would establish that the prisoner had possessed lists of His Majesty’s forces, detailing their positions and preparations on land and at sea. It would leave no doubt that he had routinely passed this information to an enemy power.

I was born in a small corner of the world surrounded by sea, a land beneath cloud shadows. When I picture the globe, with its boundless oceans and pathless continents, my native country seems an insignificant speck within that immense whole. Yet measured by intellectual power, it far outweighed nations with greater territories and much larger populations. Such was the truth that the human mind alone created everything people considered good or great, while Nature herself merely served as its chief assistant. England, far north in the restless sea, now appears in my dreams as an enormous, well-crewed ship, commanding the winds and riding proudly over the waves. As a boy, I knew her as my entire universe. Standing on the hills where I was born, I saw plains and mountains stretching to the limits of sight, dotted with my countrymen’s homes and made fertile by their work. For me, the earth’s centre lay on that spot. The rest of the globe seemed a story I could have forgotten without the slightest strain on imagination or understanding.

From the beginning, my fortunes have shown how powerfully change can shape the varied course of a human life. In my case this condition was almost an inheritance. Nature had lavished upon my father the enviable gifts of wit and imagination, then left the vessel of his life to be driven by those winds without providing reason for a rudder or judgment for a pilot. His family was obscure, but circumstances brought him to public attention early. He soon spent his modest inheritance in the brilliant world of fashionable luxury in which he played his part. During the brief years of his careless youth, the elegant idlers of the day adored him. Among his greatest admirers was the young sovereign, who escaped political intrigue and the demanding responsibilities of kingship to find unfailing amusement and renewed spirits in my father’s company. His impulses, which he never controlled, constantly drew him into trouble from which only his inventiveness could rescue him. The growing burden of gambling debts and tradesmen’s bills would have crushed anyone else, but he bore it with lighthearted, irrepressible gaiety. His presence was so essential at the dinners and gatherings of the wealthy that his failings were treated as minor faults, and he was welcomed with intoxicating praise.

Popularity of this kind, like every kind, soon fades. Meanwhile, the difficulties surrounding him multiplied at a frightening rate compared with the meagre resources he had for escaping them.
